name: Enicepatide
lead: Enicepatide (CT-388, RO7795068) is an investigational once-weekly injectable that activates both the GLP-1 and GIP receptors, developed by Roche and its subsidiary Genentech for obesity and type 2 diabetes [1][2]. It is described as signal-biased, meaning it shows minimal beta-arrestin coupling at either receptor [1].

For appearance, the relevant chain is fat loss: drugs in this class reduce appetite and body weight, and body fat has large effects on facial leanness, jaw and cheek definition and overall physique. In a phase 1 randomized trial of people with overweight or obesity it reduced body weight and was generally well tolerated, and Wikipedia cites press releases reporting 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss over 24 weeks in a later trial [1][2]. It is not approved anywhere.

Roche has registered a phase 3 programme in obesity with and without type 2 diabetes, a head-to-head comparison with tirzepatide in type 2 diabetes, a planned cardiovascular outcomes trial and a phase 2 combination with petrelintide [8][9][10][11][12]. The drug class is reviewed in a 2021 overview of emerging GLP-1-based obesity compounds [13].

paras: Enicepatide is a unimolecular peptide that activates GLP-1 and GIP receptors and whose cAMP signalling is biased at both. In cell assays both receptors showed minimal internalization compared with native ligands, and preclinical models were reported to show greater weight loss and glycaemic control with biased agonism than unbiased agonism [2]. In mice it reduced body weight, suppressed appetite and improved steatohepatitis pathology, and it improved glycaemic control in mice and monkeys [2].

GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and dual GLP-1/GIP agonists such as tirzepatide are approved for diabetes and obesity; reviews describe a wave of newer agents adding glucagon, amylin or GIP activity, with CT-388 among them [13]. A 2026 pharmacology review discusses cardiac effects of GLP-1 co-agonists [3].

The earliest human data came from a phase 1 trial registered in 2021, with a 2023 conference abstract in the journal Diabetes reporting over 8 percent weight loss in four weeks and a May 2024 Genentech press release reporting positive phase Ib results [1][4]. Phase 2 trials began in the second half of 2024, and phase 3 trials began recruiting in 2026 [8][9]. The nonproprietary name enicepatide has replaced the code CT-388 [1].

The phase 1 study (NCT04838405) was double-blind, randomized and placebo-controlled in 129 participants including adults with overweight, obesity and type 2 diabetes, testing single doses and four once-weekly doses. It reported that the drug was generally well tolerated with a safety profile consistent with other incretin-based therapies, with most treatment-emergent adverse events mild or moderate, and improved glycaemic parameters [2][4].

Two phase 2 trials are registered and listed as completed: one in 469 people with obesity or overweight and at least one weight-related comorbidity, and one in 447 with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes [5][6]. Wikipedia cites press releases reporting 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss at 24 weeks [1].

Phase 3 trials started recruiting in 2026: 2,000 participants without type 2 diabetes and 1,600 with it [8][9], plus a 300-person study with or without diabetes [7]. A 948-person trial compares it with tirzepatide in type 2 diabetes, a cardiovascular outcomes trial of 8,200 people with overweight or obesity and cardiovascular disease is planned, a phase 2 dose-finding study will test it with petrelintide, and a phase 1 study is registered in Chinese participants [10][11][12][14].

Published safety information consists of the phase 1 report of mostly mild or moderate adverse events consistent with other incretin therapies [2]. Larger trials are ongoing, so the profile at phase 3 scale has not been published.

The drug is investigational and not available by prescription. Its prominence in online discussion follows that of tirzepatide and other incretin drugs among people pursuing fat loss. Because it is unapproved, any product sold under its name outside trials would be unregulated.

quick.overview:
Enicepatide is a weekly injectable that activates GLP-1 and GIP receptors, from Roche. It is in phase 3 for obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Wikipedia cites 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss at 24 weeks in a trial.
quick.mechanism: A signal-biased dual agonist of GLP-1 and GIP receptors with minimal beta-arrestin coupling.
quick.risks: Investigational and unapproved; published safety information is limited.

chain: Less body fat, leaner face and physique
angle.text: Incretin-based drugs lower appetite and weight, and people who lose body fat commonly describe a leaner face and a more defined physique. Enicepatide is still in trials, so any such outcome would depend on the results of its phase 3 programme.
